findings: [prose-quality] “the twenty-six houses above it are due to be lit on Thursday” -> “the twenty-six houses above the vessel are due to be lit on Thursday” : read aloud, one sentence binds it twice to two referents: the bottom of it is the lane, above it is the vessel. The second it re-binds silently.

[prose-quality] “It is a coating on it, a passenger, and passengers can get off.” -> “It is a coating on the fuel, a passenger, and passengers can get off.” : It is the warning and it is the fuel inside one seven-word clause; the epigram lands only if the ear can split them.

[prose-quality] “a serviceable molecule that is no use as a warning, because it hardly smells” -> “a perfectly stable molecule that is no use as a warning, because it hardly smells” : collocation near-miss: serviceable means fit for use, and the same clause denies use. The intended sense is chemically sound, not useful.

[prose-quality] “The buried plastic that replaced most of the country’s old iron takes almost none of it.” -> “The buried plastic that replaced most of the country’s old iron takes almost none of the smell.” : it reaches back two paragraphs to the mercaptan; the nearest noun a reader has in hand is the gas, which is the wrong one.

[prose-quality] “and slow gas gives up more than fast gas, which on a new estate makes it worse” -> “and slow gas gives up more than fast gas, and on a new estate the gas is slow” : which takes a clausal antecedent and it takes none; the load-bearing step (a new estate draws little, so the gas is slow) is left for the reader to supply.

[prose-quality] “the further it has travelled against that wall” -> “the further it has travelled against that oxide” : that wall is a demonstrative definite on first mention in the body; the noun is licensed only by the title, three paragraphs above the reader’s eye.
justification: Read aloud end to end, passage and every limb with two sentences either side. The instrument, the mechanism and the inversion all carry. Six findings, all prose quality, none touching a key: five are pronoun or definite-reference slips and one is a collocation near-miss on serviceable. Nothing teaches against its own key; the direction-of-surprise clause (bare oxide takes the most, so a main scrubs hardest in the week it goes into service) states the counter-intuitive direction correctly and paragraph three repeats it as the pipe that needs watching is the pipe nobody has ever used. No quoted sentence is swallowed by a host copula anywhere in this unit: all 24 citations are colon- or verb-introduced fragments.

findings: [prose-quality] “five at the farm office halfway up” -> “five at the smallholding halfway up” : the same farm carries a new-run reading of five and, through the old steel line that has fed the farm buildings since the sixties, a reading of three. justification: Read aloud, passage and all four limbs with two sentences either side. Nothing teaches the opposite of its key: the closing paragraph states the mechanism’s direction explicitly - partials sit above the whole-number multiples rather than below them, so the octave finishes wide and not narrow - which is exactly the direction a careless writer inverts.

findings: [prose-quality] “He gave up the circuit in 1903” -> “Inglebeck gave up the circuit in 1903” : He reaches back over nine intervening sentences, none of which contains a single human referent - they are all mileages, markets, charters and coaches. By the time the pronoun arrives the reader has been in a gazetteer for a hundred words.

[prose-quality] “which served the three towns” -> “which served Haddenthorpe, Nerresby and Thrapmere” : the three towns is a definite-with-numeral on first mention. The card has named four places and the reader is not told until the NEXT sentence that the Shenwolds are off the road. The definite is resolvable only backwards, and option B turns on which places the road served.

[prose-quality] “the Thursday market is the largest of the four” -> “the Thursday market is the largest on the card” : the four presupposes four markets, but only two have been named at that point (Thrapmere’s Wednesday and Lower Shenwold’s Thursday); Haddenthorpe’s and Nerresby’s arrive two sentences later. The out-of-order arrival is deliberate and good; the definite numeral that depends on it is not.

[prose-quality] “The first is the card, printed as ” -> “The first is the card: ” : the host copula swallows the quoted sentence. The first is the card, printed as ... is terminated by the quotation’s own borrowed full stop, and the citation is not colon-introduced, so the host sentence has no stop of its own.
justification: Read aloud, passage and all four limbs with two sentences either side. The essay’s trick - print the card, then let the market days arrive out of order two sentences apart so the reader has to sort them - is well made and the mileages are exact (nine to Nerresby, thirty on to Thrapmere of which twenty-one lie beyond Haddenthorpe: 9 + 21 = 30). Four findings, all prose quality: one long pronoun reach, two definites that presuppose what the reader has not yet been given, and one host clause swallowing a quoted sentence. Nothing teaches the opposite of its key.

findings: [correctness] “Nerresby is the near neighbour, nine miles out” -> “Nerresby is the nearer of the two other market towns, nine miles out” : contradicted by the passage’s own mileages. The two Shenwolds lie four miles from Haddenthorpe against Nerresby stands nine miles from Haddenthorpe, so Nerresby is not the near neighbour - the Shenwolds are, at less than half the distance. A student who checks the limb against the map the essay gives him finds it wrong. The key is unaffected: D still falls on the Thursday market is the largest of the four.

[prose-quality] “A is put together from two places in the essay that are never brought together.” -> “A is right, and it is assembled from two places in the essay that are never brought together.” : the rationale never affirms its key. The only explicit verdict in the unit is B is the strong wrong answer; A is described but never called right, where every sibling opens with an affirmation (C is right. / The gap takes Worse (D). / Option D is the key). The replacement also removes the put together / brought together repetition inside eleven words.
justification: Mechanical sweep. (a) Limb-faces-option: all four limbs re-read against the option each faces. B (the coach road settled who went on the card) is met head-on - the essay builds the coach-road case first, then the Thursday undoes it, because two places three miles off the road up a lane the coaches did not use keep their place on the card anyway. C (two markets on the Thursday) is killed by one sentence, Upper Shenwold has no market of its own. D (Nerresby drew the biggest crowd) is killed on the essay’s single weighing of the markets. No limb faces an option it does not have. (b) Quoted spans: 10 extracted between U+201C and U+201D and tested for substring membership against the exact passage string; 10 of 10 byte-identical, 0 failures. (c) Contradiction sweep: the road distances reconcile exactly and the four-town/four-day mapping is one-to-one with no town holding two days, which is what makes the key sound. ONE CORRECTNESS DEFECT: the D limb calls Nerresby the near neighbour when the passage puts the Shenwolds at four miles and Nerresby at nine. Tagged for repair. One further finding, prose quality: the rationale never states that A is the key.

findings: [prose-quality] “on a Thursday”, and then, two sentences later, ” -> “on a Thursday”, and, two sentences later, ” : two parallel citations of complete passage sentences inside one host sentence are punctuated differently: the first is cut before its stop (comma outside), the second carries its stop inside. Both reproduce their cut faithfully, so this is not a rule violation, but on the page the pair looks inconsistent. Cutting the second before its stop as well would settle it.

[prose-quality] “C reads the Thursday as two markets where there is one” -> “\n\nC reads the Thursday as two markets where there is one” : all four limbs are packed into one 300-word block, where the batch’s other multi-limb units give each limb its own paragraph. The C and D limbs are effectively unfindable for a learner scanning for the option he picked. Break before C and again before D.

[prose-quality] “the Thursday market is the largest of the four” -> “the Thursday market was the largest of the four” : register, not error: this passage carries exactly ONE copular predicate in eleven sentences (0.09 per sentence) against an authentic ELF minimum of 0.17 and a median of 0.51. Everything else stands, lies, sits, fills, keeps, holds, gives up or takes. The result reads as a gazetteer rather than an essay. The fix is not this substitution but the addition of one or two copular predicates elsewhere; the string is cited because it is the single one the passage has.
